data.title: Fox–Fordyce disease — viva
data.summary: Acne & appendageal disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Fox–Fordyce disease** (Acne & appendageal disorders)_

**Q1. What is Fox–Fordyce disease?**
- Chronic, intensely itchy papular eruption of apocrine gland-bearing areas ('apocrine miliaria') due to keratin plugging of the apocrine duct in the follicular infundibulum with duct rupture; women 13–35 years; worsened by heat, sweating, stress, menstruation; improves in pregnancy and with OCPs/after menopause

**Q2. Clinical features.**
- Dome-shaped skin-coloured to slightly yellow/hyperpigmented follicular papules in axillae (commonest), areolae, pubic and perineal areas, periumbilical
- Intense itch, decreased apocrine sweating, sparse axillary hair
- Reported after laser hair removal

**Q3. Discuss apocrine and eccrine glands (PYQ).**
- Eccrine: distributed all over (palms/soles most), open directly on skin, cholinergic sympathetic innervation, merocrine secretion of watery hypotonic sweat — thermoregulation
- Apocrine: axillae, anogenital, areola, ear canal (ceruminous), eyelids (Moll's glands); open into hair follicle above sebaceous duct; adrenergic innervation; functional after puberty; viscous secretion — odour after bacterial action (bromhidrosis)
- Apoeccrine glands: axillae in adults, mixed features — hyperhidrosis

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Infundibular hyperkeratosis plugging the apocrine duct, spongiosis of the follicular infundibulum, perifollicular xanthomatous (foamy) macrophages (characteristic), lymphocytic infiltrate, dilated apocrine glands

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Lichen nitidus, lichen planus, folliculitis, syringomas, miliaria, Darier's disease, lichen amyloidosis, acanthosis nigricans, hidradenitis suppurativa (early), periductal mastitis (areola)

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Avoid heat/sweating; loose clothing
- Topical: steroids, clindamycin, tretinoin/adapalene, calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus/tacrolimus), aluminium chloride (limited)
- Systemic: combined OCPs, isotretinoin, botulinum toxin injections, oral antihistamines; procedures — electrocoagulation, fractional laser, liposuction-curettage, surgical excision for severe localised disease

**Q7. Dermoscopy findings.**
- Perifollicular translucency, keratin plugs in follicles, loss of hair shafts, yellowish background — helps support diagnosis

**Q8. Fox–Fordyce after laser hair removal — mechanism.**
- Thermal damage to the follicular infundibulum leads to keratin plugging of apocrine ducts — reported weeks to months after laser hair removal of axillae

**Q9. Topical and procedural treatments in detail.**
- Topical: clindamycin, tretinoin/ adapalene (unplug ducts), steroids (mid-potency), tacrolimus/ pimecrolimus, benzoyl peroxide; botulinum toxin (reduces apocrine secretion — good results); microwave/ liposuction curettage, electrocautery, fractional CO2 laser, surgical excision in refractory cases
- Systemic: OCPs, isotretinoin (case reports)

**Q10. Compare eccrine and apocrine glands (PYQ).**
- Eccrine: everywhere (palms/soles most), open directly onto skin, merocrine, watery sweat for thermoregulation, cholinergic sympathetic innervation, present from birth
- Apocrine: axillae, anogenital, areolae, eyelids (Moll), ear canal (ceruminous); open into hair follicle above sebaceous duct; decapitation secretion; viscous odourless secretion (odour from bacteria); active after puberty; adrenergic innervation

**Q11. What is chromhidrosis?**
- Coloured sweat (yellow, green, blue, black) — apocrine (lipofuscin) on face/ axillae; eccrine (dyes/ drugs — clofazimine, rifampicin); pseudochromhidrosis (bacterial/ chromogenic); treat with capsaicin, botulinum toxin

**Q12. Differential diagnosis.**
- Syringomas, lichen nitidus, lichen planus, folliculitis, eruptive vellus hair cysts, milia, periumbilical perforating pseudoxanthoma elasticum, apocrine miliaria

**Q13. Pathogenesis.**
- Keratin plugging of the intra-infundibular part of apocrine ducts → rupture → apocrine sweat retention and inflammation; hormonal (begins after puberty, improves in pregnancy and after menopause); can follow laser hair removal of axillae

**Q14. Describe the clinical presentation in detail.**
- Young women (13–35 y): intensely itchy, dome-shaped, skin-coloured to yellowish follicular papules in apocrine areas — axillae (commonest), areolae, pubic/ labial region, periumbilical; worse with heat, emotion, exercise; reduced axillary sweating and sparse hair

**Q15. Enumerate apocrine gland disorders.**
- Fox–Fordyce disease, hidradenitis suppurativa (now considered follicular), apocrine bromhidrosis (malodour — bacterial breakdown), chromhidrosis (coloured sweat — lipofuscin), apocrine hidrocystoma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum, extramammary Paget's disease, apocrine carcinoma

## Quick spotter facts
- Itchy follicular axillary papules in a young woman, worse with sweating — Fox–Fordyce
- Perifollicular foamy macrophages

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Disorders of apocrine glands). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
